product.title: Russian 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Russian: a stressed pronunciation guide printed right above every Cyrillic word, short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Russian builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a Cyrillic alphabet table, the rules of vowel reduction, a summary of the six cases, A1 verb tables, and a glossary. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from sentences with no word for "is" to past-tense verbs that change with the speaker's gender.

cover_design.label: RUSSIAN
cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Russian for complete beginners — from reading Cyrillic in one sitting to telling the story of last weekend.
cover_design.catatan: A stressed pronunciation guide above every word, and a word-for-word translation under every line of dialogue.

blocks.text: Russian has a scarier reputation than it deserves. The first thing people see is the alphabet — a row of backwards letters and symbols that look like a code — and they stop right there and decide the language is out of reach. Yet Cyrillic is actually the **easiest** part of the whole journey. Thirty-three letters, one letter one sound, almost without exception. Most people who take it seriously can read Cyrillic haltingly in one afternoon and fluently within a week. Compare that with English, where *though*, *through*, *tough* and *thought* use the same letters for four different sounds.

The really hard part lies elsewhere, and this course won't pretend otherwise. Russian changes **the endings of its nouns** according to the job the word does in the sentence. In English, "Moscow" stays "Moscow" whether it's the subject, the destination or the location: *Moscow is big*, *I'm going to Moscow*, *I'm in Moscow*. In Russian all three sound different: Москва, в Москву, в Москве. That system is called case, and it's what makes beginners give up most often — not the alphabet.

The good news: at A1 you don't need to master the whole system. You need the six cases in the singular, mostly only in their most common patterns, and about three hundred words. With that you can introduce yourself, order food, bargain at a market, ask for directions, describe your day and talk about yesterday. This course is built so that the cases arrive **one at a time, once you need them**, not as a six-column table on page three that makes people close the book.

Three things are deliberately different from other Russian courses. First, **the pronunciation is printed above each Cyrillic word, with the stressed syllable in CAPITAL LETTERS**. Stress is not decoration in Russian: it changes the vowel sounds across the whole word, and a word with the wrong stress is often not recognized at all by native speakers. Second, every line of dialogue has a **word-for-word translation** that shows the original structure, including when that structure sounds odd in English — because that's exactly where the lesson is. Third, each unit targets **one typical mistake learners make**, and it's named openly, not hidden in a footnote.

One last thing. Russian isn't a language you can soak up quietly through series and songs the way many people pick up English or Korean. There's no reservoir of things you've half-heard waiting to be tapped. Everything you'll have is what you build yourself, page by page. That sounds heavy, but there's an upside: there are no bad habits to undo first. We start from a clean zero.

This course has twenty units. Each unit is designed for one sitting — about twenty to thirty minutes — and contains one dialogue, notes on that dialogue, one to three grammar boxes, vocabulary, four exercises and their answers. If you do one unit a day, you'll finish in three weeks. Three units a week, in seven weeks. Both are fine; what isn't fine is doing five units in one day and then stopping for a month.
How to work through a unit

items: **Read the dialogue once, only the Cyrillic and the pronunciation.** Don't look at the translation. The aim isn't to understand, but to get your eyes and mouth used to it. Say it out loud — Russian has many consonant clusters that will never become easy if you only read them in your head.
**Read it again with the translation and the literal line.** The literal line is the heart of this course. It shows that *У меня есть брат* really says "at-me is brother", not "I have a brother".
**Read the notes.** That's where the trouble spots mentioned in the foreword live.
**Do the exercises without looking back.** Write by hand if you can; writing Cyrillic by hand forces your brain to take the letters apart one by one.
**Check against the key, then read the dialogue once more.** The same dialogue will feel different after the exercises.

blocks.title: Three ground rules
items: **Don't skip the pages on stress and vowel reduction.** The next two pages decide whether your Russian sounds like Russian or like someone reading a shopping list.
**Don't memorize the case tables at the back yet.** Those pages are for *checking*, not *learning*. Cases come in through sentences, not tables.
**Say everything out loud.** Russian has sounds that English doesn't (ы, щ, soft consonants). Not one of them can be mastered with your eyes.

front.title: Cyrillic: thirty-three letters in three piles

blocks.text: The fastest way to master Cyrillic isn't to memorize the alphabet in order, but to sort it into three piles: letters you already know, letters that **pretend** to be ones you know, and letters that are truly new. The first pile is free, the third takes practice, and the second is where all the mistakes happen.
Pile 1 — same shape, same sound (free)
Pile 2 — familiar shape, deceptive sound ⚠️
These letters are the ones that most often make beginners read a Russian word completely wrong. Give them extra attention; if needed, write them on a separate card.
Pile 3 — new shapes
The rest. The shapes are new, but most of the sounds exist in English, so all you need to practice is recognizing the shapes. The full table is on the next page.

blocks.title: Three letters that need special care
items: **Ы ы** — a vowel between *ee* and *oo*. Say the *i* of *bit* while pulling your tongue back as if about to say *oo*, lips unrounded. In this course it's written **y**: сын = *syn* (son). Ы really does tell words apart: мышь (*mysh'*, mouse) versus мишь, which is not a word.

**Щ щ** — a long, soft *sh*, like *sh ch* in *fresh cheese* run together, or a held *sh* with the tongue raised. In this course it's written **shch**: борщ = *borshch*. The difference from Ш (*sh*) is subtle; native speakers hear it, and you'll get there.
**Ж ж** — like the *s* in *measure*, or the *zh* in *Zhivago*. Not English *j* (which sounds *dzh*). In this course it's written **zh**: жена = *zhy-NA* (wife).

blocks.text: Thirty-three letters, in alphabetical order. The "Say it" column uses the spelling found consistently throughout this course. Cover the right-hand columns with paper and test yourself until nothing trips you up.

blocks.title: Four spelling rules that apply from day one
items: **Voiced final letters become voiceless.** Б→п, В→ф, Г→к, Д→т, Ж→ш, З→с at the end of a word. So хлеб (bread) is said *khlep*, not *khleb*. Муж (husband) is said *moosh*.
**Ё is always stressed.** If you see ё, the stress of that word is right there. Unfortunately, real Russian texts often print ё as е — in this course it's always written in full.
**-ого / -его are said -ova / -eva.** The г in these endings is said **v**, not g. его (him) = *ye-VO*. This isn't a random exception; the pattern is fixed.

**Ь softens; it isn't pronounced.** брат (*brat*, brother) versus брать (*brat'*, to take): the second т is said with the tongue pressed closer to the roof of the mouth, as if about to add a faint *y*.

front.title: Stress: the one thing that changes everything

blocks.text: If you only read one of the introductory pages, read this one. English has stress too (*REcord* vs *reCORD*), but Russian takes it much further: stress decides **the sound of every vowel in the word**, and a word with the wrong stress is often simply not recognized.
Rule one: unstressed О sounds like A

This single law changes your reading more than anything else. The letter о only sounds like *o* when it's stressed. In other syllables it weakens to *a* — and the further from the stress, the vaguer it gets.

head: Written
Say it
Meaning
Why
rows: the first two о weaken to *a*, the third is stressed

blocks.text: Beginners almost always read *ho-ro-sho* and *mo-lo-ko*, because that's how the letters are written. Russians will understand — once. But it clearly sounds foreign. Make it a habit from day one: **see о, check the stress, if it's unstressed say a**.
Rule two: unstressed Е and Я sound like I
Rule three: stress can move when a word changes form

⚠️ This is why stress can't be learned once and done. Compare: **ру**ка (ROO-ka? no — *roo-KA*, hand) but its plural **ру**ки (*ROO-ki*). Дом (*dom*, house) has the plural дома (*da-MA*). That's why in this course **every word in the dialogues and vocabulary tables carries its own pronunciation**, including words that have appeared before. Don't treat it as wasteful repetition — the stress may have moved.

blocks.title: How to learn stress without memorizing
items: **Learn each word together with its stress, never separately.** Store *ma-la-KO* in your head, not м-о-л-о-к-о with the stress added later. A word that goes in without its stress almost always goes in with the wrong one.
**Make stressed syllables LONGER, not just louder.** That's the biggest difference between an English accent and natural Russian sound — English tends to punch the stress, Russian stretches it.
**If you're unsure and have nothing to check, guess the second-to-last syllable for long words.** Not a rule — just the guess that's right most often. Then check.

blocks.text: Singular noun endings — the most common patterns

blocks.title: Three things that save beginners
items: **Masculine INANIMATE nouns don't change in the accusative.** Я читаю журнал — журнал is exactly the dictionary form. So half the objects you'll use are free.
**Masculine ANIMATE nouns use the genitive form as the accusative.** Я знаю **брата** (I know (my) brother), not брат. This is the only place at A1 where "alive or not" matters.
**The feminine dative and prepositional are both -е.** книге for both. One ending, two cases, half the memorizing.

blocks.text: Present — two groups
Past — follows gender and number, not person ⚠️

⚠️ The number-one trap for learners: the past tense doesn't care whether you're *я*, *ты* or *он* — it cares about **the speaker's gender**. A woman who says *я был* immediately sounds wrong. A woman says **я была**.
Future — two ways

head: Form
Pattern
Example
rows: Я **буду работать**. — I will work / be working.
the present-tense form of a perfective verb

blocks.text: Aspect — the pairs you need at A1
Numbers 0–20
Tens and hundreds

blocks.title: The number decides the form of the noun ⚠️
items: Ending in **1** (except 11): ordinary singular — 21 рубл**ь**, 1 час.
Ending in **2, 3, 4** (except 12–14): genitive singular — 22 рубл**я**, 3 час**а**.
Ending in **5–20, 0**: genitive plural — 25 рубл**ей**, 5 час**ов**.
The same pattern applies to год/года/лет (year) and минута/минуты/минут.

If you've reached this page after working through twenty units, you have something real: Cyrillic you can read without spelling it out, about three hundred active words, six cases in the singular, present and past tense verbs, and the ability to handle everyday business — introducing yourself, ordering, asking the way, shopping, describing your day. That is genuine A1, not A1 in name only.
The three most useful things to do now

items: **Reread every dialogue from Unit 1 onward, back to back, over two days.** Unit 1 will feel almost silly — proof that the course works. More importantly, you'll catch patterns you couldn't see the first time.

**Start writing five sentences a day about your own day.** Not textbook exercises: sentences about your life. *Сегодня я работал дома. Вечером я смотрел фильм.* The mistakes that show up there are your real mistakes, and those are the fastest to fix.

**Find someone to talk to before you feel ready.** There will never be a "ready" moment. Three hundred words are enough for a first halting conversation, and those halting conversations are what take you to A2.

blocks.title: A parting word
items: Russian pays you back later. The first six months feel like climbing without a view; then one day a long sentence reaches your ear and you understand all of it without translating. That day comes for everyone who sticks with it.
Удачи! (oo-DA-chi) — Good luck.
До свидания! (da svi-DA-ni-ya) — Goodbye.
